title: Reliability — Electricity 2026
date_evidence: The report was published by the International Energy Agency in February 2026, with the metadata showing February 6, 2026 as the publication date.
key_claim: Power systems face rising risks from ageing infrastructure, extreme weather events, cyberthreats and other emerging vulnerabilities; large-scale outages hit Chile, the Iberian Peninsula and Mexico in 2025; in Iraq, temperatures of nearly 50 degrees C led to the shutdown of two transmission lines and a nationwide blackout on 11 August 2025 with a sudden loss of more than 6,000 MW.
notes: Tier 1 multilateral. Structural anchor (3-6m band): the canonical 2026 reliability assessment that reframes the binding risk toward extreme weather. Cited inline like any other source. IEA report pages are JS-rendered; date and reliability-chapter content captured via WebSearch of the publisher and exact title plus the report PDF.

title: 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment
date_evidence: I found information about NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment that was recently released in May 2026. ... NERC concludes that all assessment areas are expected to have adequate resources to meet normal summer peak demand in 2026.
key_claim: All assessment areas are expected to have adequate resources to meet normal summer peak demand in 2026, and more than 58 GW of new generation has been added since summer 2025; but three subregions (NPCC-New England, MRO-SaskPower, WECC-Northwest) face elevated risk of supply shortfalls under above-normal or extreme conditions, and extreme heat, drought, wildfires and hurricanes can simultaneously reduce generation and increase demand, with extreme heat the primary threat.
verbatim_quote: simultaneously reduce generation and increase demand
notes: Tier 1 primary reliability assessment. NERC PDF did not return content via WebFetch; release date and findings captured via WebSearch of the publisher and exact title and corroborated by RTO Insider coverage dated 19 May 2026.

title: Extended heat wave could cripple New York's grid this summer: NYISO
date_evidence: meta-date: 2026-04-28 ; meta-article_date_original: Tuesday, April 28, 2026, 10:00 AM ; Published April 28, 2026
key_claim: NYISO's annual summer reliability assessment (24 April 2026) found a baseline reliability margin of just 417 MW, the lowest in recent history and down from 1,918 MW in 2022; 34,615 MW of resources are available against forecast peak demand of 31,578 MW; under a three-day-or-longer heatwave averaging 95 degrees F the capacity margin is forecast at -1,679 MW, and at 98 degrees F at -3,370 MW, before emergency actions that can free 3,166 MW.
notes: Tier 3 specialist trade press reporting NYISO's primary summer reliability assessment. Used for the quantification anchor showing a margin that is adequate at baseline but deeply deficient under correlated heat stress.

title: NERC overstates reliability risks in long-term assessment: Grid Strategies
key_claim: Grid Strategies, in a report released 9 March 2026 for Earthjustice, NRDC, the Sierra Club and the Environmental Defense Fund, argues NERC's long-term reliability assessment is too pessimistic: it pairs a high data-center demand forecast with conservative generation and interregional-flow assumptions, and counting likely-to-connect queued resources and non-firm interregional flows resolves the majority of identified seasonal adequacy shortfalls; non-firm imports were critical during Winter Storm Uri, when MISO imported 13 GW.
notes: Tier 3 trade press reporting the Grid Strategies counter-analysis. Used as the sourced disconfirmation for the Counter-Argument box.

publisher: arXiv (Dubus, Troccoli, Zuiker and Stoop; RTE, WEMC, ENTSO-E, TenneT)
title: Leveraging Climate Services to Build Climate Resilient Power Systems
key_claim: Traditional energy-system modelling uses historical reanalysis datasets that are by construction representative only of past conditions, and their validity for long-term adequacy studies diminishes as the climate system departs from historical norms; compound hazards such as simultaneous heatwaves and droughts affect both demand and hydropower, and large-scale circulation patterns create correlated weather across countries that reduces the effectiveness of geographic diversification; ENTSO-E and the Copernicus Climate Change Service have built the projection-based PECD4.2 dataset to underpin the ERAA 2026 and TYNDP 2026, while RTE's 2025 SDDR plan reinforces grid sections in flood, heatwave and drought zones and prepares for +2.7 degrees C of warming in France by 2050.
verbatim_quote: diminishes as the climate system departs from historical norms
notes: Tier 2 academic paper authored by transmission-system operators and climate-service institutions (paper submitted to CIGRE Paris Session 2026). Anchors the methodological pivot from historical to forward-looking climate data in adequacy planning.

title: Climate Intuition: Demand is here, time to build the grid of tomorrow
date_evidence: Climate Intuition: Demand is here, time to build the grid of tomorrow ... March 25, 2026
key_claim: Around $5.8 trillion of cumulative grid investment is forecast globally between 2026 and 2035, with about $1 trillion in the US over the coming decade; much of the developed-world grid was built in the 1960s and 1970s and is nearly 60 years old, and the aging grid is a national security risk, more likely to fail and vulnerable to extreme weather; resilience-related keyword frequency in S&P 1500 utilities' meeting transcripts has risen 70% since 2016, and wholesale power prices in the US and Europe surged 30-40% in the past year.
verbatim_quote: The aging grid is a national security risk
notes: Tier 2 major-institution climate-advisory research (J.P. Morgan Climate Advisory, Dr Sarah Kapnick). Anchors the scale of the grid build and the decision-relevance of resilience for investors.

title: Distributed Energy Can Unleash the Resilient, Affordable Grid of the Future
date_evidence: Report April 28, 2026 Distributed Energy Can Unleash the Resilient, Affordable Grid of the Future
key_claim: The US power system is at a pivotal moment: rising demand from manufacturing, data centers and electrification is straining an aging grid largely built in the 1960s and 1970s (70% of transmission lines were at least 25 years old by 2023), and increasingly severe and frequent extreme weather - hurricanes, heat and cold waves, wildfires and floods - is raising reliability concerns; distributed energy resources orchestrated as virtual power plants can cut peak demand and defer or avoid costly traditional infrastructure investment.
notes: Tier 2 research organisation. Corroborates the aging-infrastructure and extreme-weather exposure and anchors distributed energy and demand flexibility as a structural adaptation.
